title: The Sun is a star
description: The Sun is an ordinary star (the closest one to Earth), not a special category of object.

facts.text: The Sun is a star, and it is the closest star to Earth.
The other stars visible at night are also stars like the Sun; they look like points of light because they are much farther away.

title: Earth is the third planet
description: Our solar system has eight planets; Earth is the third from the Sun.

facts.text: The solar system has eight planets.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
The solar system is the Sun plus everything that orbits it.

title: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
description: Light from the Sun takes roughly eight minutes to cross the distance to Earth, so we always see the Sun slightly in the past.

facts.text: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth.

title: The Milky Way is our galaxy
description: The Sun is one of more than a hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.

facts.text: The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in the Milky Way.
The faint band of light across a dark night sky is the Milky Way, seen from inside it.
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy.

title: The Sun runs on nuclear fusion
description: In its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that becomes sunlight.

facts.text: The Sun's core is about 15 million °C.
The Sun generates energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.

title: The Sun holds almost all the mass
description: About 99.8% of the solar system's mass is in the Sun.

facts.text: The Sun contains about 99.8% of the mass of the solar system, leaving about 0.2% for the planets, moons, asteroids and comets.

title: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old
description: The Sun formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago.

facts.text: The Sun is roughly halfway through its life and has enough hydrogen to keep fusing for billions of years more.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.

title: The four rocky planets
description: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small, rocky inner planets.

facts.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the rocky inner planets, made mostly of rock and metal.

title: Venus is the hottest planet
description: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

facts.text: Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system, with a surface temperature over 450 °C.
Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.
Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

title: Why Mars is red
description: Mars looks red because iron oxide, better known as rust, coats its dust and rocks.

facts.text: Mars looks red because of iron oxide (rust) in its soil, rocks and dust.
Fine red dust in the thin Martian atmosphere contributes to the planet’s reddish color.
Mars’s red color comes from iron oxide, the same compound as rust, in its dust and rocks.

title: Gas giants and ice giants
description: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

facts.text: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
The gas giants are made mostly of hydrogen and helium and have no solid surface.
The ice giants are rich in water, ammonia and methane “ices” and are smaller than the gas giants.

title: Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined
description: Jupiter is the largest planet and has more than twice the mass of all the others put together.

facts.text: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

title: Saturn's rings are ice
description: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, with some rock.

facts.text: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice with some rock.
Saturn's ring particles range from dust-sized grains to chunks as big as a house.

title: Seasons come from Earth's tilt
description: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun.

facts.text: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, and this tilt causes the seasons.
In summer, sunlight strikes a hemisphere more directly and days are longer; in winter, sunlight arrives at a lower angle and spreads out.

title: Seasons aren't about distance
description: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

facts.text: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
The Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons.

title: What causes Moon phases
description: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us; the cycle takes about 29.5 days.

facts.text: The Sun always lights half of the Moon; phases depend on how much of that sunlit half we can see from Earth.
A full cycle of Moon phases takes about 29.5 days.

title: The Moon always shows us the same face
description: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.

facts.text: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.
The Moon is on average about 384,400 km from Earth.
The far side of the Moon is not permanently dark; it receives as much sunlight as the near side.

title: Solar vs lunar eclipses
description: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.

facts.text: In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, and the Moon's shadow falls on Earth.
In a lunar eclipse Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
Solar eclipses can only happen at new Moon, and lunar eclipses only at full Moon.

title: The 400× coincidence
description: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

facts.text: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so both look about the same size in our sky.
During a total solar eclipse the Moon covers the Sun's bright disc, revealing its faint outer atmosphere (the corona).

title: A light-year is a distance
description: A light-year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km.

facts.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km.
Light travels about 300,000 km every second, faster than anything else.
Light takes just over one second to travel from the Moon to Earth.

title: The nearest star after the Sun
description: Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away, is the closest star to the Sun.

facts.text: The closest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.

title: A star's color is its temperature
description: Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest.

facts.text: A star's color shows its surface temperature: blue-white stars are the hottest and red stars the coolest.
The Sun is intermediate in temperature, which is why it appears white-yellow.

title: Stars are born, age and die
description: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust. The Sun will swell into a red giant and end as a white dwarf; massive stars can explode as supernovae.

facts.text: Stars form in collapsing clouds of gas and dust.
The Sun is not massive enough to explode as a supernova.
The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
Stars much more massive than the Sun can end their lives in a supernova that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
In about 5 billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and end as a white dwarf.

title: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across
description: Our galaxy is about 100,000 light-years from edge to edge.

facts.text: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across.

title: Andromeda, our big neighbor
description: Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.

facts.text: Andromeda can be seen with the naked eye from a dark site as a faint smudge.
The Andromeda galaxy, the nearest large spiral galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.

title: Billions of galaxies, 13.8 billion years
description: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies and is about 13.8 billion years old.

facts.text: The observable universe contains billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.

title: Earth’s spin makes day and night
description: Earth rotates on its axis about once every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day.

facts.text: Earth rotates on its axis about once every 24 hours, and this spin gives us day and night.
At any moment, the half of Earth facing the Sun has daytime and the half facing away has night.
Earth’s axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles that Earth spins around.

title: Why everything rises in the east
description: Earth spins west to east, so the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

facts.text: Earth rotates from west to east, so the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.
At the equator, Earth’s surface moves at about 1,670 km/h because of Earth’s rotation.
We don’t feel Earth’s spin because we, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed.

title: A year is one orbit
description: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, moving at about 30 km per second.

facts.text: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once; that orbit is a year.
Earth travels around the Sun at about 30 km per second.
In one orbit Earth travels roughly 940 million km.

title: Why leap years exist
description: The extra quarter-day in each orbit adds up, so the calendar adds a day about every four years.

facts.text: Calendar years have 365 days but an orbit takes about 365.25 days, so calendars add an extra day (February 29) about every four years to stay in step with the seasons.

title: The night sky changes with the seasons
description: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.

facts.text: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side of Earth faces different parts of space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.
Orion is a prominent evening constellation in Northern Hemisphere winter.

title: What constellations are
description: Constellations are patterns of stars and, officially, 88 regions that together cover the whole sky.

facts.text: The International Astronomical Union officially recognizes 88 constellations.
Officially, each constellation is a region of the sky with set boundaries, and together they cover the whole sky.
Constellations began as patterns of stars that people named after figures, animals and objects.

title: Constellation stars aren’t neighbors
description: Stars in the same constellation are usually at very different distances and only line up from our viewpoint.

facts.text: The stars in a constellation are usually at very different distances from Earth and only appear close together from our viewpoint.

title: Asterisms: patterns within constellations
description: Familiar star patterns like the Big Dipper are asterisms, not official constellations.

facts.text: The Big Dipper is not an official constellation; it is an asterism, part of the constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear).

title: The North Star marks north
description: Polaris sits almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves and marks north.

facts.text: Polaris, the North Star, lies almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it stays nearly fixed while other stars circle around it.
Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky; Sirius is.
In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris’s height above the horizon in degrees is roughly equal to your latitude.
The Southern Hemisphere has no bright pole star; navigators have used the Southern Cross to find south.

title: Stars that never set
description: Stars close to the celestial pole circle it and, from mid-northern latitudes, never dip below the horizon.

facts.text: From mid-northern latitudes, stars near Polaris circle it and never set; these are called circumpolar stars.

title: Earth’s wobble changes the pole star
description: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles over about 26,000 years, so the pole star changes over millennia.

facts.text: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, tracing a circle about every 26,000 years, so Polaris won’t always be the pole star.

title: The ecliptic
description: The Sun’s yearly path across the sky; the Moon and planets stay close to it because the solar system is flat.

facts.text: The ecliptic is the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky over a year.
The Moon and planets always appear close to the ecliptic because their orbits lie in nearly the same flat plane.
The constellations along the ecliptic are the zodiac constellations.
The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so eclipses only happen when a new or full Moon occurs near where the Moon’s path crosses the ecliptic.

title: Planets wander against the stars
description: Planets shift position against the background stars from night to night; “planet” comes from the Greek for wanderer.

facts.text: The word “planet” comes from the ancient Greek word for “wanderer,” because planets drift against the background stars.

title: Retrograde motion
description: Planets sometimes appear to move backwards against the stars because Earth overtakes or is overtaken by them.

facts.text: Mars and the other outer planets sometimes appear to move backwards against the stars for a while when Earth, on its faster inner orbit, overtakes them.
Retrograde motion is only apparent: the planets never actually reverse direction in their orbits.

title: The Moon drives the tides
description: The Moon’s gravity pulls Earth’s oceans into two bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day.

facts.text: Ocean tides are caused mainly by the Moon’s gravity, with a smaller contribution from the Sun.
The Moon’s pull creates two bulges of water, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth.
As Earth rotates through the two bulges, most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

title: Spring and neap tides
description: When the Sun and Moon line up tides are larger (spring); at right angles they are smaller (neap).

facts.text: Spring tides, the largest tidal ranges, happen around new and full Moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up.
Neap tides, the smallest tidal ranges, happen around first and last quarter Moon, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles.
Spring tides have nothing to do with the season of spring; they happen twice a month.

title: The giant-impact origin of the Moon
description: The leading explanation is that the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.

facts.text: The leading explanation for the Moon’s origin is that a Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the debris.
The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago.
Scientists call the hypothesized Mars-sized impactor Theia.

title: Evidence from Moon rocks
description: Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle and the Moon has only a small iron core, consistent with the giant impact.

facts.text: The Moon has only a small iron core compared with Earth.
Computer simulations of a giant impact can produce a Moon with an Earth-like composition and a small iron core.
Moon rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts are chemically very similar to rocks from Earth’s mantle.

title: Lunar craters
description: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by impacts and survive for billions of years because the Moon has no air, water or plate tectonics to erase them.

facts.text: The Moon’s craters were made by asteroids and comets striking its surface.
Lunar craters range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers across.
Lunar craters last for billions of years because the Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics to wear them away.

title: The Moon’s dark “seas”
description: The dark patches on the Moon are maria: huge plains of ancient solidified lava, not water.

facts.text: The dark patches on the Moon, called maria (Latin for “seas”), are vast plains of ancient lava that cooled and hardened.
Most of the maria are on the Moon’s near side, the side that faces Earth.

title: Every sky motion has a cause
description: Daily motion comes from Earth’s spin, yearly changes from Earth’s orbit, and the Moon’s motion and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

facts.text: Because Earth also moves along its orbit, each star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night, adding up to a different night sky over the year.

title: The sky as the first calendar
description: Ancient cultures tracked the Sun, Moon and stars to mark seasons, plan farming and hold ceremonies.

facts.text: Stonehenge in England is aligned with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.
Ancient Egyptians linked the first dawn appearance of Sirius each year with the start of the Nile’s annual flood.
Babylonian astronomers recorded the positions of the Moon and planets on clay tablets and used the records to predict eclipses.

title: Navigating by the stars
description: Before instruments, navigators crossed oceans by memorizing where stars rise and set.

facts.text: Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometers of open Pacific Ocean using the rising and setting points of stars, along with ocean swells and wildlife.

title: Eratosthenes measures Earth
description: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared noon shadows in two Egyptian cities to estimate Earth’s circumference.

facts.text: At Syene on the summer solstice, the noon Sun shone straight down a deep well, while in Alexandria it cast a shadow about 7° from vertical, about 1/50 of a circle; so the distance between the cities was about 1/50 of Earth’s circumference.
Eratosthenes’ estimate was remarkably close to the modern value of about 40,000 km, though how close depends on the length of the ancient stadion he used.
Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared the Sun’s noon angle in two Egyptian cities, Syene and Alexandria, to estimate Earth’s circumference.

title: Ancient scholars knew Earth is round
description: Greek thinkers had evidence Earth is a sphere, such as its curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses.

facts.text: Earth’s shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse is always curved, which ancient Greek thinkers such as Aristotle took as evidence that Earth is round.

title: The Earth-centered model
description: For centuries, most scholars placed a motionless Earth at the center, with Ptolemy’s model using small circles (epicycles) to fit planetary motion.

facts.text: Around 150 CE, Ptolemy described an Earth-centered (geocentric) model of the universe in a book later known as the Almagest.
Ptolemy’s model explained retrograde motion by having each planet move on a small circle (an epicycle) that itself moved around Earth.
Ptolemy’s model predicted the positions of the planets accurately enough to be used for calendars and astronomy for centuries.
The geocentric model was the dominant view in Europe and the Middle East for about 1,400 years.

title: Why an Earth-centered view made sense
description: We don’t feel Earth moving, and no one could detect stars shifting as Earth orbited.

facts.text: A major reason the geocentric model seemed sensible is that people cannot feel Earth moving.
If Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should shift slightly over a year; ancient observers could not detect this shift (parallax), which seemed to support a motionless Earth.

title: The Sun-centered model
description: Copernicus placed the Sun at the center, with Earth as one of the planets orbiting it.

facts.text: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus published a Sun-centered (heliocentric) model in which Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.
The heliocentric model explains retrograde motion simply, as Earth overtaking the outer planets, without epicycles as its cause.
Copernicus still assumed perfectly circular orbits, so his model needed extra small circles to match observations.
Aristarchus of Samos had proposed a Sun-centered arrangement around 1,800 years before Copernicus.

title: Galileo’s telescope discoveries
description: From 1609–1610 Galileo turned a telescope to the sky and found evidence that not everything circles Earth.

facts.text: Galileo did not invent the telescope, which first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, but he built improved ones and turned them on the sky in 1609.
In 1610 Galileo discovered four large moons orbiting Jupiter, now called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Galileo saw that Venus shows a full set of phases like the Moon, which the Ptolemaic model could not explain but a Sun-centered model could.
Galileo’s telescope showed mountains and craters on the Moon and revealed the Milky Way to be made of countless stars.

title: Kepler’s laws
description: Planets orbit in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are.

facts.text: Johannes Kepler worked out his laws using the precise naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe.
Kepler’s first law: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.
Kepler’s second law: a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun.
Kepler’s third law: the farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer it takes to complete an orbit.

title: Newton’s law of gravity
description: One force, universal gravitation, explains falling objects, the Moon’s orbit and Kepler’s laws.

facts.text: In 1687 Isaac Newton published his law of universal gravitation in the Principia.
Newton showed that the same force that makes objects fall on Earth also holds the Moon in orbit and the planets around the Sun.
In Newton’s law, gravity grows with the masses of the objects and weakens with the square of the distance between them.
Gravity at the Moon’s surface is about one-sixth of Earth’s, so a person would weigh about one-sixth as much there.
Newton’s law of gravity explains why Kepler’s laws work.

title: The astronomical unit
description: The average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km, is the yardstick of the solar system.

facts.text: The astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance between Earth and the Sun, about 150 million km.
Kepler’s laws gave the relative distances of the planets, but astronomers still needed one real distance to set the scale.
Astronomers observed the transits of Venus across the Sun in 1761 and 1769 from around the world to measure the Earth–Sun distance.
Today the astronomical unit is known very precisely thanks to radar measurements and spacecraft.
Mars orbits about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth does (about 1.5 AU).

title: The discovery of Uranus
description: William Herschel found Uranus in 1781, the first planet discovered with a telescope.

facts.text: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet discovered using a telescope.
Before 1781, astronomers had recorded Uranus several times but mistaken it for a star.

title: Neptune found by mathematics
description: Irregularities in Uranus’s orbit led astronomers to predict Neptune’s position; it was found there in 1846.

facts.text: Neptune was found in 1846 after mathematicians, notably Urbain Le Verrier, predicted its position from unexplained tugs on Uranus’s orbit.
Johann Galle spotted Neptune within about 1° of Le Verrier’s predicted position.

title: Proof that Earth moves
description: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured stellar parallax, direct evidence that Earth orbits the Sun.

facts.text: Stellar parallax is a direct observation of Earth’s motion around the Sun, answering an objection that had stood for about 2,000 years.
In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of the star 61 Cygni, the first measured distance to a star.

title: The electromagnetic spectrum
description: Visible light is one small band of a spectrum that runs from radio waves to gamma rays; all of it is light traveling at the same speed.

facts.text: The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays.
Visible light is only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
All kinds of electromagnetic radiation, from radio waves to gamma rays, travel through space at the speed of light.
What distinguishes radio waves, visible light and X-rays is their wavelength: radio waves are longest and gamma rays shortest.
Human eyes detect light with wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometers.
Some animals, such as bees, can see ultraviolet light that is invisible to humans.
In visible light, red light has the longest wavelength and violet light the shortest.

title: Spectral fingerprints
description: Each element absorbs and emits its own set of colors, so a spectrum reveals what a star is made of.

facts.text: Spectra show that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
Each chemical element absorbs and emits light only at its own specific set of wavelengths, called spectral lines.
By spreading starlight into a spectrum and matching its lines, astronomers can tell which elements a star contains.

title: Helium was found in the Sun first
description: Helium was discovered in the Sun’s spectrum in 1868, before it was found on Earth; its name comes from the Greek word for Sun.

facts.text: Helium was first detected in 1868 as an unexplained line in the Sun’s spectrum, before it was found on Earth.
Helium is named after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.

title: Refractors and reflectors
description: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes use mirrors, and all the largest telescopes are reflectors.

facts.text: Refracting telescopes gather light with lenses; reflecting telescopes gather it with curved mirrors.
Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope, in 1668.
The largest telescopes are reflectors, because big lenses sag under their own weight while mirrors can be supported from behind.

title: Bigger is better
description: A telescope’s light-gathering area sets how faint it can see and how fine the detail it can show.

facts.text: A telescope with a larger mirror or lens collects more light, so it can see fainter objects and finer detail.
The largest optical telescopes operating today have mirrors about 10 meters across, and telescopes with mirrors more than 30 meters wide are under construction.
Very large telescope mirrors are often built from many smaller segments fitted together.

title: The atmosphere gets in the way
description: Earth’s moving air blurs starlight (stars twinkle) and blocks much of the spectrum, which is why some telescopes go to space.

facts.text: Stars twinkle because turbulence in Earth’s atmosphere bends their light back and forth.
Earth’s atmosphere blocks most ultraviolet light and X-rays, and much infrared, from reaching the ground.

title: The Hubble Space Telescope
description: Launched in 1990, Hubble orbits above the atmosphere and has made some of astronomy’s sharpest images.

facts.text: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990.
Hubble orbits Earth above the atmosphere, so its images are free of atmospheric blurring.
Hubble’s observations helped pin down the age of the universe at about 13.8 billion years.
Hubble is the only space telescope designed to be repaired and upgraded by astronauts in orbit.

title: Radio astronomy
description: Radio telescopes detect long-wavelength radio waves, which pass through dust and can be observed day and night.

facts.text: Radio telescopes are often huge dishes because radio waves are very long, and a bigger dish is needed to see fine detail.
Radio waves pass through cosmic dust and Earth’s clouds, and radio telescopes can observe during the day.
In the early 1930s Karl Jansky detected radio waves coming from the Milky Way, founding radio astronomy.
Radio telescopes can be linked into arrays that work together like one much larger telescope.
The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 radio dishes that can be spread over up to 36 km.

title: Infrared astronomy
description: Infrared light passes through dust, revealing hidden star birth, and captures light from the most distant galaxies.

facts.text: Infrared light is the kind of radiation we feel as heat.
Infrared light passes through clouds of dust that block visible light, revealing stars forming inside them.
Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched by the expanding universe into infrared wavelengths.

title: The James Webb Space Telescope
description: Launched in 2021, Webb is a huge infrared telescope with a 6.5-meter gold-coated mirror, orbiting the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.

facts.text: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021.
Webb’s main mirror is 6.5 meters across and made of 18 gold-coated segments.
Webb’s five-layer sunshield is about the size of a tennis court.
Webb orbits the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth, behind a sunshield that keeps it extremely cold.

title: An orbit is falling around
description: A spacecraft in orbit is falling toward Earth but moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing.

facts.text: An object in orbit is constantly falling toward Earth, but it moves sideways fast enough that Earth’s surface curves away beneath it.
The International Space Station orbits at about 28,000 km/h, circling Earth about every 90 minutes.
Astronauts float in orbit because they and their spacecraft are falling together, not because there is no gravity.

title: Escape velocity
description: To leave Earth completely, a spacecraft must reach about 11.2 km per second.

facts.text: Escape velocity from Earth’s surface is about 11.2 km per second (about 40,000 km/h).

title: The Voyager probes
description: Launched in 1977, the twin Voyagers toured the giant planets; Voyager 1 is now in interstellar space.

facts.text: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 were launched in 1977.
Voyager 1 reached interstellar space in 2012 and is the most distant human-made object.
Each Voyager carries a Golden Record of sounds and images from Earth.
Voyager 1 is so far away that its radio signals take more than 20 hours to reach Earth.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).

title: The Apollo Moon landings
description: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings between 1969 and 1972, bringing back 382 kg of samples.

facts.text: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon.
Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings between 1969 and 1972.
The last astronauts to walk on the Moon, on Apollo 17, left it in December 1972.
Astronauts’ footprints on the Moon can last for a very long time because the Moon has no wind or rain to wear them away.
The Apollo missions brought back 382 kg of Moon rocks and soil.

title: Each kind of light tells a different story
description: Astronomers combine radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-ray views, each revealing different objects.

facts.text: X-ray telescopes reveal extremely hot gas, such as the gas around black holes and in galaxy clusters.
X-ray telescopes must work in space because Earth’s atmosphere absorbs X-rays.
NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory was launched in 1999.

title: Mercury: extremes without air
description: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun, Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it swings from scorching days to frigid nights.

facts.text: Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system and the closest to the Sun.
Mercury orbits the Sun in 88 Earth days, the shortest year of any planet.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere to trap heat.
Mercury’s surface reaches about 430 °C in the day and falls to about −180 °C at night.
Despite its heat, Mercury has water ice in craters near its poles that are always in shadow.

title: Venus: Earth’s twin in size only
description: Venus is nearly Earth’s size but has crushing pressure, acid clouds and a backwards rotation.

facts.text: Venus is nearly the same size as Earth.
The air pressure at Venus’s surface is about 90 times that at Earth’s surface.
Venus is covered by thick clouds of sulfuric acid.
Venus rotates backwards compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun rises in the west.
Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once, longer than its 225-day year.
Soviet Venera landers reached Venus’s surface in the 1970s and 1980s but survived only up to about two hours.

title: What protects life on Earth
description: Earth’s magnetic field deflects charged particles from the Sun, and its atmosphere and ozone layer shield the surface.

facts.text: Earth’s magnetic field is generated by molten iron moving in its outer core.
Earth’s magnetic field deflects most of the charged particles streaming from the Sun.
Earth’s atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
The ozone layer high in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet light.
About 71% of Earth’s surface is covered by water.
Earth is the only planet known to have life.
Charged particles from the Sun that reach the upper atmosphere near the poles make the sky glow as auroras.

title: Mars once had water
description: Dry river valleys and lake beds show that liquid water once flowed on Mars; today its water is frozen.

facts.text: Mars has a thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide, with less than 1% of Earth’s surface air pressure.
Dried river valleys and ancient lake beds show that liquid water once flowed on Mars.
NASA’s Curiosity rover, which landed in 2012, found that Gale Crater once held a lake.
Today most of Mars’s water is frozen, in its polar ice caps and underground.
Mars has Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system.
NASA’s Perseverance rover landed in 2021 in Jezero Crater, the site of an ancient lake and river delta, and is collecting rock samples.

title: The asteroid belt
description: A wide ring of rocky and metallic asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that never formed a planet.

facts.text: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Jupiter’s gravity stirred up the material in the asteroid belt and kept it from forming a planet.
All the asteroids in the main belt together have less mass than Earth’s Moon.
Most asteroids are made of rock, and some are made largely of metal.
The asteroid belt is mostly empty space; spacecraft have crossed it without hitting anything.
Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, is classified as a dwarf planet.

title: Jupiter’s storms and moons
description: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth; its four large moons are worlds in their own right.

facts.text: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a giant storm wider than Earth that has been observed for more than 150 years.
Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the solar system and is bigger than the planet Mercury.
Jupiter’s moon Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
The Great Red Spot has been shrinking over the past century.
Jupiter has dozens of known moons; the four Galilean moons are by far the largest.
Jupiter’s moon Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered worlds in the solar system.

title: Ocean worlds
description: Some icy moons, like Europa and Enceladus, hide oceans of liquid water beneath their ice, kept liquid by tidal heating.

facts.text: Jupiter’s moon Europa has a salty liquid-water ocean beneath its icy shell, which may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans.
NASA’s Cassini spacecraft saw plumes of water ice spraying from cracks near the south pole of Saturn’s moon Enceladus.
The gravity of their giant planets squeezes and flexes moons like Europa and Enceladus, heating their interiors enough to keep water liquid.
NASA’s Europa Clipper mission launched in 2024 to study Europa and its ocean.
Liquid water, a source of energy and the right chemistry are key ingredients for life as we know it, which is why ocean worlds interest scientists.

title: Titan
description: Saturn’s largest moon has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.

facts.text: Titan is Saturn’s largest moon and is bigger than the planet Mercury.
Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, made mostly of nitrogen.
Titan has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane, and it rains methane.
Titan’s surface is about −179 °C, far too cold for liquid water.
Besides Earth, Titan is the only world known to have stable liquid on its surface.
In 2005 the Huygens probe landed on Titan, the first landing on a world in the outer solar system.

title: Uranus and Neptune up close
description: Uranus is tipped on its side; Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system; methane makes both blue.

facts.text: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it essentially orbits the Sun on its side.
Because of its tilt, each of Uranus’s poles gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.
Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, reaching more than 2,000 km/h.
Methane in the atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune absorbs red light, giving them their blue color.
Neptune takes about 165 years to orbit the Sun once; it completed its first orbit since its discovery in 2011.

title: The size of the solar system
description: The planets span about 30 astronomical units; sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.

facts.text: Neptune orbits about 30 astronomical units from the Sun, about 4.5 billion km.
Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.

title: Dwarf planets and Pluto
description: In 2006 the IAU defined a planet as clearing its orbital neighborhood; Pluto doesn’t, so it’s a dwarf planet.

facts.text: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that orbits the Sun, is massive enough to be round, and has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.
Pluto meets the first two conditions but has not cleared its orbital neighborhood, so it is classified as a dwarf planet.
The IAU recognizes five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh.
In 2015 NASA’s New Horizons flew past Pluto and revealed a huge heart-shaped region covered in nitrogen ice.

title: The Kuiper Belt
description: A vast ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto and the source of many comets.

facts.text: The Kuiper Belt is a doughnut-shaped region of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Pluto is one of the largest known objects in the Kuiper Belt.
The Kuiper Belt is similar to the asteroid belt but far larger: about 20 times as wide and many times as massive.
In 2019 New Horizons flew past Arrokoth, a small Kuiper Belt object and the most distant object ever explored up close; it is thought to be largely unchanged since the planets formed.
Many comets that return every few decades or centuries come from the Kuiper Belt.

title: Comets
description: Comets are icy bodies that grow a glowing head and tails when they near the Sun; their tails always point away from it.

facts.text: Comets are made of ice, dust and rock, often described as “dirty snowballs.”
When a comet nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas, forming a glowing cloud called a coma and long tails.
A comet’s tails always point away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind.
Many comets have two tails: one of dust and one of charged gas (ions).
Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years; it last passed Earth in 1986 and will be back in 2061.

title: Meteoroids, meteors and meteorites
description: A meteoroid is space debris, a meteor is its streak of light in our sky, and a meteorite is what reaches the ground.

facts.text: A meteoroid is a small piece of rock or debris in space; a meteor is the streak of light it makes burning up in Earth’s atmosphere; a meteorite is any piece that reaches the ground.
Most meteors come from particles about the size of a grain of sand.
Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through the trail of debris left by a comet.
The Perseid meteor shower peaks every August, when Earth crosses debris from Comet Swift–Tuttle.

title: The Oort Cloud
description: A vast, distant shell of icy bodies thought to surround the solar system, the source of long-period comets.

facts.text: The Oort Cloud is thought to be a giant spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system.
The Oort Cloud may extend as far as 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun.
No object in the Oort Cloud has ever been directly observed there; its existence is inferred from long-period comets.
Comets that take thousands of years or more to orbit the Sun are thought to come from the Oort Cloud.
Even Voyager 1 will take about 300 years to reach the inner edge of the Oort Cloud.

title: Inside the Sun
description: Energy made in the Sun’s core travels out through the radiative and convective zones to the photosphere; the corona above is far hotter.

facts.text: From the inside out, the Sun’s main layers are the core, the radiative zone, the convective zone, the photosphere (its visible surface), the chromosphere and the corona.
The Sun’s visible surface, the photosphere, is about 5,500 °C.
The Sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona, is over 1 million °C, far hotter than the surface below it.
Energy made in the Sun’s core can take many thousands of years to work its way out to the surface.
Why the corona is so much hotter than the Sun’s surface is still not fully understood.

title: Sunspots and the solar cycle
description: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically active regions whose number rises and falls over an ~11-year cycle.

facts.text: Sunspots are regions of the Sun’s surface that are cooler, and so darker, than their surroundings, caused by intense magnetic fields.
The number of sunspots rises and falls in a solar cycle that lasts about 11 years.
Galileo was among the first to observe sunspots with a telescope, in the early 1600s.
Near solar minimum, the Sun can go for days with no visible sunspots.
Galileo used the movement of sunspots across the Sun’s face to show that the Sun rotates.

title: Solar storms and space weather
description: The solar wind and eruptions like flares and coronal mass ejections cause auroras and can disrupt technology.

facts.text: The Sun constantly blows a stream of charged particles into space, called the solar wind.
Solar flares are sudden bursts of radiation, and coronal mass ejections hurl huge clouds of charged particles into space.
Strong solar storms can disrupt satellites, radio communications and power grids on Earth.
The Carrington Event of 1859 is the most intense solar storm on record; it produced auroras seen far from the poles.

title: How the solar system formed
description: About 4.6 billion years ago a spinning cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the Sun and a flat disk that built the planets.

facts.text: As the cloud collapsed it spun faster and flattened into a disk, with the Sun forming at the center; that is why the planets orbit in nearly the same plane.
Close to the young Sun it was too hot for ices to form, so rocky planets formed there; farther out, ices could condense, letting the giant planets grow large.
The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a cloud of gas and dust collapsed under its own gravity.

title: The heliosphere
description: The solar wind blows a bubble around the solar system; Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

facts.text: The solar wind blows a vast bubble around the Sun and planets called the heliosphere.
Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the outer edge of the heliosphere, in 2012, entering interstellar space.

title: Measuring star distances with parallax
description: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star.

facts.text: As Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against more distant stars; this shift is called parallax.
The closer a star is, the larger its parallax shift, so measuring the shift gives its distance.
A parsec, the distance at which a star’s parallax would be one arcsecond, is about 3.26 light-years.
The European Space Agency’s Gaia spacecraft has measured the positions and distances of more than a billion stars.

title: Brightness versus luminosity
description: How bright a star looks depends on its true output and its distance; brightness fades with the square of distance.

facts.text: How bright a star looks from Earth depends both on how much light it actually gives off (its luminosity) and on how far away it is.
A star’s apparent brightness falls with the square of its distance: twice as far away, it looks a quarter as bright.
Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is both more luminous than the Sun and relatively close, about 8.6 light-years away.

title: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
description: A chart of stars’ luminosity against temperature; most fall on a diagonal band, the main sequence.

facts.text: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots stars by their luminosity and their surface temperature.
The diagram is named after Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, who developed it independently in the early 1900s.
Most stars, including the Sun, fall along a diagonal band on the diagram called the main sequence.
The Sun sits near the middle of the main sequence: an average star in temperature and luminosity.
Red giants appear in the upper right of the diagram (cool but very luminous) and white dwarfs in the lower left (hot but dim).

title: A star’s mass sets its life
description: On the main sequence, more massive stars are hotter and brighter but burn out far faster.

facts.text: A main-sequence star is one fusing hydrogen into helium in its core; stars spend most of their lives this way.
The more massive a main-sequence star is, the hotter, brighter and shorter-lived it is; the most massive last only a few million years.
The smallest, coolest stars, red dwarfs, use fuel so slowly that they can shine for trillions of years.
The Sun will spend about 10 billion years in total on the main sequence.
Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is a red dwarf.

title: Binary stars
description: Many stars orbit partners; watching their orbits lets astronomers weigh stars.

facts.text: Many stars orbit a companion star; the Sun, which is single, is not typical in this respect.
The nearest star system, Alpha Centauri, has three stars, including Proxima Centauri.
Some binary stars pass in front of each other as seen from Earth, so their combined light dims regularly; these are called eclipsing binaries.
Measuring how two stars orbit each other lets astronomers calculate their masses using the laws of gravity.
Sirius has a small, faint companion, Sirius B, which is a white dwarf.

title: Where stars are born
description: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together until fusion ignites.

facts.text: Stars form inside cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together until their cores become hot enough for fusion.
The Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest large region of star formation and is visible to the naked eye in the sword of Orion.
Hubble photographed the “Pillars of Creation,” towering columns of gas and dust where stars are forming in the Eagle Nebula, in 1995.

title: Red giants and planetary nebulae
description: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, it swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers as a glowing planetary nebula.

facts.text: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, its core contracts and heats up while its outer layers swell into a red giant.
As a red giant, the Sun is expected to grow large enough to engulf Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth.
Late in life, a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers into a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula.
A planetary nebula glows for only tens of thousands of years before it fades.
Planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets; early astronomers named them because they looked like planets’ disks through small telescopes.

title: White dwarfs
description: The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about the size of Earth, with much of the Sun’s mass, slowly cooling.

facts.text: A white dwarf is the exposed core of a Sun-like star, about the size of Earth but with a mass comparable to the Sun’s.
Most stars in the Milky Way, including the Sun, will end their lives as white dwarfs.
White dwarf material is so dense that a teaspoonful would weigh several tons on Earth.
A white dwarf no longer fuses anything; it shines with leftover heat and slowly cools over billions of years.

title: Supernovae and star stuff
description: Massive stars explode as supernovae, scattering elements forged inside stars, including those in our bodies.

facts.text: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun end their lives when their cores collapse, triggering a supernova.
In 1987 a supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way, was visible to the naked eye.
Nearly all elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were made by nuclear reactions inside stars and in stellar explosions.
The calcium in our bones and the iron in our blood were made inside stars that lived and died before the Sun formed.

title: Mass decides a star’s fate
description: Low-mass stars end as white dwarfs; the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

facts.text: A star’s final fate depends mainly on its mass: Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs, while the most massive stars explode and leave behind neutron stars or black holes.

title: Neutron stars
description: The collapsed core left by a supernova: about 20 km across yet more massive than the Sun.

facts.text: A neutron star is the collapsed core left behind when a massive star explodes as a supernova.
A neutron star is only about 20 km across, about the size of a city, yet can hold more mass than the Sun.
Neutron star material is so dense that a teaspoonful would weigh billions of tons on Earth.
Many neutron stars spin many times per second and have magnetic fields far stronger than Earth’s.
Neutron stars are made mostly of neutrons packed tightly together.

title: Pulsars
description: Rapidly spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.

facts.text: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams of radio waves; when a beam sweeps past Earth, we see a pulse, like a lighthouse.
The first pulsar was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, then a graduate student.
Some pulsars spin hundreds of times every second.
The Crab Nebula is the remains of a supernova that Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054; a pulsar spins at its center.
The first pulsar’s signal was so regular that its discoverers half-jokingly nicknamed it “LGM,” for “little green men.”

title: Black holes
description: A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape; formed when very massive stars collapse.

facts.text: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
Stellar black holes form when the core of a very massive star collapses at the end of its life.
From a safe distance, a black hole’s gravity is the same as that of any object with the same mass; it does not suck in everything around it.

title: The event horizon
description: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can return; the EHT imaged a black hole’s shadow in 2019.

facts.text: A black hole’s event horizon is the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape.
In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole, the one at the center of the galaxy M87.
The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes around the world so they work like one Earth-sized telescope.
The black hole in M87 has a mass about 6.5 billion times that of the Sun.

title: The black hole at the center of the Milky Way
description: Sagittarius A* holds about 4 million times the Sun’s mass; stars orbiting it revealed it.

facts.text: Astronomers found Sagittarius A* by tracking stars that orbit an invisible, extremely massive object at the galaxy’s center.
One star near the galactic center, called S2, completes an orbit around Sagittarius A* about every 16 years.
Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the supermassive object at our galaxy’s center.
In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released an image of Sagittarius A*.
Sagittarius A* is about 27,000 light-years from Earth.
The Milky Way’s central black hole, Sagittarius A*, has a mass about 4 million times that of the Sun.

title: Gravitational waves
description: Ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein and first detected by LIGO in 2015 from merging black holes.

facts.text: Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicted gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, in 1916.
LIGO’s detectors can measure changes in length far smaller than the width of a proton.
The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the detection of gravitational waves.
In 2017 astronomers detected gravitational waves and light from two merging neutron stars, a collision that forged heavy elements such as gold.
LIGO first detected gravitational waves on September 14, 2015, from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away.

title: Finding exoplanets
description: Most exoplanets are found by the dips in starlight they cause (transits) or the wobble they give their stars.

facts.text: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun.
In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, earning the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The wobble method finds planets by the slight back-and-forth motion their gravity causes in their star, measured through shifts in the star’s spectrum.
More than 5,000 exoplanets have been confirmed.
NASA’s Kepler space telescope used the transit method to discover thousands of exoplanets.
The transit method finds planets by the small, regular dip in a star’s light when a planet passes in front of it.

title: The habitable zone
description: The range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface; closer in for dim stars.

facts.text: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet’s surface could be the right temperature for liquid water.
Around dimmer, cooler stars the habitable zone lies much closer to the star; around brighter stars it lies farther out.
TRAPPIST-1, a red dwarf about 40 light-years away, has seven Earth-sized planets, several of them in its habitable zone.
Being in the habitable zone does not guarantee liquid water or life; a planet’s atmosphere matters too.

title: The search for life
description: Scientists look for biosignatures on Mars and ocean moons and in exoplanet atmospheres, and SETI listens for signals.

facts.text: Scientists search exoplanet atmospheres for biosignatures, gases such as oxygen and methane together, that living things could produce.
SETI projects search for radio and other signals that could have been made by technological civilizations.
No life has yet been confirmed anywhere beyond Earth.
The James Webb Space Telescope can analyze starlight passing through some exoplanets’ atmospheres to detect the gases they contain.

title: Three stellar remnants
description: White dwarfs are Earth-sized, neutron stars city-sized, and black holes have no surface at all.

facts.text: A white dwarf is about the size of Earth, a neutron star about the size of a city, and a black hole has no surface at all, only an event horizon.

title: Kinds of galaxies
description: Galaxies come as spirals, ellipticals and irregulars, a scheme Edwin Hubble introduced.

facts.text: Galaxies are commonly classified as spiral, elliptical or irregular, a scheme introduced by Edwin Hubble in the 1920s.
Spiral galaxies have a flat, rotating disk with spiral arms where young stars are forming.
Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars with little new star formation.
Irregular galaxies have no clear shape; the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are examples.

title: The structure of the Milky Way
description: A barred spiral with a central bulge, spiral arms, and a halo; the Sun orbits the center about every 230 million years.

facts.text: The Milky Way has a central bulge, a flat disk with spiral arms, and a surrounding halo of old stars and globular star clusters.
The Sun lies about 26,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way, in a minor spiral arm.
The Sun takes about 230 million years to orbit the center of the Milky Way once.
Since it formed, the Sun has completed only about 20 orbits of the Milky Way’s center.

title: Galaxy collisions
description: Galaxies collide and merge; the Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

facts.text: Galaxies can collide and merge, reshaping each other over hundreds of millions of years.
When galaxies collide, individual stars almost never hit each other, because the space between stars is so vast.
The Andromeda galaxy is moving toward the Milky Way and the two are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

title: The Local Group
description: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda, with dozens of smaller galaxies.

facts.text: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, a gathering of more than 50 galaxies dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda.
The Local Group is about 10 million light-years across.
The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.

title: Dark matter
description: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter; an unseen mass, dark matter, outweighs ordinary matter about five to one.

facts.text: In the 1970s Vera Rubin’s measurements of how galaxies rotate provided strong evidence for dark matter.
In 1933 Fritz Zwicky found that galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held together by their visible mass.
There is roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter in the universe.
Dark matter does not give off, absorb or reflect light; it is detected only through its gravity.
Stars at the edges of galaxies orbit so fast that the visible matter alone could not hold them in; extra unseen mass must be present.
What dark matter is made of is still unknown.

title: Galaxy clusters and gravitational lenses
description: Galaxies gather in clusters whose gravity bends and magnifies the light of galaxies behind them.

facts.text: Galaxies are gathered into clusters that can contain hundreds or thousands of galaxies, bound together by gravity.
The gravity of a massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies light from galaxies behind it, acting as a gravitational lens, as Einstein’s relativity predicts.
Webb’s first deep-field image, released in 2022, used a galaxy cluster as a gravitational lens to reveal much more distant galaxies.

title: Quasars and active galaxies
description: When a galaxy’s central supermassive black hole feeds, its glowing disk can outshine the whole galaxy: a quasar.

facts.text: Most large galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their center.
When a supermassive black hole pulls in large amounts of gas, the gas heats up in a swirling disk and can outshine the entire galaxy; such an object is called a quasar.
The first quasar was identified in 1963, when Maarten Schmidt found that the object 3C 273 was extremely distant and luminous.
Quasars are among the most distant and luminous objects known.

title: Hubble’s expanding universe
description: Hubble showed that other galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way and that they are moving away from us, faster the farther they are.

facts.text: In 1924 Edwin Hubble showed that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy far beyond the Milky Way.
Georges Lemaître had proposed the expanding universe and the relation between distance and speed a few years before Hubble’s paper.
The expansion has no center: galaxies are moving apart because space itself is expanding, so every galaxy sees the others receding.
In 1929 Hubble reported that galaxies are moving away from us at speeds that increase with their distance, evidence that the universe is expanding.

title: Redshift
description: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths; the farther the galaxy, the bigger the redshift.

facts.text: Redshift is the stretching of light to longer, redder wavelengths, seen as a shift of spectral lines toward the red.
As light travels across expanding space, its wavelength is stretched, so light from distant galaxies arrives redshifted.
The more distant a galaxy is, the greater its redshift.

title: The cosmic web
description: On the largest scales, galaxies form a web of filaments and sheets around vast, nearly empty voids.

facts.text: On the largest scales, galaxies and clusters are arranged in a web of long filaments and sheets surrounding huge, nearly empty voids.

title: The Big Bang
description: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

facts.text: The Big Bang theory says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
The Big Bang was not an explosion into empty space; it was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once.
In its first few minutes, the young universe formed the lightest elements: hydrogen, helium and small traces of lithium.
The name “Big Bang” was coined in 1949 by astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favored a rival theory.
The Big Bang theory describes how the universe evolved from a hot, dense early state; it does not explain what, if anything, came before.

title: The cosmic microwave background
description: The Big Bang’s leftover light, released about 380,000 years after it began and stretched into microwaves by the expansion.

facts.text: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is a faint glow of microwaves that fills the whole sky: leftover light from the early universe.
The CMB was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe had cooled enough for atoms to form; before then it was too hot and dense for light to travel far.
The CMB began as the glow of hot gas; the expansion of the universe has since stretched that light into microwaves.
The CMB today has a temperature of about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero (2.7 K).
The CMB was discovered by accident in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who at first suspected a fault in their radio antenna.
The Big Bang theory predicted a leftover glow like the CMB, so its discovery became key evidence for the theory.

title: The first stars and galaxies
description: After the cosmic dark ages, the first stars, made of only hydrogen and helium, lit up within a few hundred million years.

facts.text: After the CMB was released, the universe went through the “cosmic dark ages,” a long stretch before the first stars formed.
The first stars are thought to have formed within a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.
The first stars formed from only hydrogen and helium and are thought to have been very massive and short-lived.
The first generations of stars made the first heavier elements and scattered them into space when they died.
Webb has observed galaxies as they were only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

title: Dark energy
description: In 1998 astronomers found the expansion of the universe is speeding up; the unknown cause is called dark energy.

facts.text: Before 1998, astronomers expected gravity to be slowing the expansion of the universe.
In 1998 two teams studying distant supernovae found them fainter than expected, showing that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.
Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the accelerating expansion.
Dark energy makes up roughly 68% of the universe’s energy content and dark matter about 27%; ordinary matter is only about 5%, so about 95% is dark.
What dark energy is remains unknown; the name refers to whatever is making the expansion accelerate.

title: The observable universe
description: We can only see as far as light has traveled since the Big Bang; expansion makes that region about 93 billion light-years across.

facts.text: Because light takes time to travel, looking at distant objects means seeing them as they were in the past.
The most distant light we see set out about 13.8 billion years ago, but space has expanded since, so the regions that sent it are now much farther than 13.8 billion light-years away.
The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across.
The observable universe is the part we can see, limited by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang; it is not the edge of the universe.
How big the whole universe is, and whether it is infinite, is unknown.

title: From atoms to galaxies
description: Big Bang gas formed stars; stars forged heavier elements and returned them to space, where they built new stars, planets and people.

facts.text: Matter is recycled across cosmic history: gas from the Big Bang formed stars, stars forged heavier elements and returned them to space, and that enriched gas formed new stars, planets and eventually people.

title: How we know what we know
description: Most astronomical knowledge comes from reading the light and other signals the universe sends us.

facts.text: Almost everything we know about stars and galaxies comes from studying the light and other signals they send, since we can visit only a few nearby worlds.

title: Futures of the Sun, Earth and universe
description: Earth’s axis will point away from Polaris, the Sun will brighten and swell, galaxies will merge, and accelerating expansion will carry distant galaxies from view.

facts.text: The Sun is slowly getting brighter; in roughly 1 billion years it is expected to make Earth too hot for liquid-water oceans.
If dark energy keeps accelerating the expansion, galaxies beyond our local neighborhood will eventually move out of view.

title: The big open questions
description: Dark matter, dark energy, the Hubble tension, what came before the Big Bang, and life elsewhere remain unsolved.

facts.text: Different ways of measuring how fast the universe is expanding today give slightly different answers, a puzzle known as the Hubble tension.
